title: Rearranging a series
objectives: See why rearranging a conditionally convergent series can change its sum.

screens.title: The greedy rule
screens.prose: The **greedy rule** for a target $T$: $$\text{total} \le T \Rightarrow \text{next unused positive term}; \quad \text{total} > T \Rightarrow \text{next unused negative term.}$$ It uses every term once, so it is a **rearrangement** of the series.
screens.question: For $T = 0$, starting from a total of 0, what are the first four terms?

options.why: You started with a negative. A total of 0 is at most $T = 0$, so the rule takes a positive first.
You alternated as in the original order. After $-\tfrac12$ the total 0.5 is still above 0.
You switched back too soon. After $-\tfrac14$ the total is 0.25, still above 0.

hints.text: 0 is at most 0, so the first term is positive.
After 1 the total is above 0, so take negatives until it is not.
$1 - \tfrac12 - \tfrac14 = 0.25 > 0$, so the fourth term is $-\tfrac16$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the rule at each step, with $T = 0$.

Because each positive term is larger than the negative term before it.

Finitely many. Removing finitely many terms from a divergent series leaves it divergent.

screens.title: The overshoot shrinks
screens.prose: Just before a crossing the total was on one side of $T$. One term carried it to the other side.
screens.question: After that crossing, how far from $T$ can the total be?

At most $\tfrac12$, the largest negative term.

hints.text: Before the crossing term, the total was on the near side of $T$.
So the total and $T$ both lie within that one term's jump.
The terms tend to 0, and every term is used eventually.

screens.title: Any target, proved
screens.prose: Assemble the proof that the greedy rearrangement of $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ converges to $T$. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: The positive terms alone add to $\infty$, and the negative terms to $-\infty$.
So the totals cross $T$ infinitely often, and every term is used, each exactly once.
Between crossings the total stays within the size of the term that made the last crossing.
The terms tend to 0, so these sizes tend to 0, and the totals tend to $T$. $\blacksquare$
The series converges, so every rearrangement converges to the same sum.
lines.why: You assumed order cannot matter. That holds for absolutely convergent series only.

lines.text: Each step moves the total closer to $T$.
lines.why: You expected steady progress. From 1.5333, adding $-\tfrac12$ gives 1.0333, further from 1.5.

Divergent halves give crossings; the shrinking terms give the squeeze.
Order: both halves diverge, crossings and every term used, the overshoot bound, then the limit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Prove the crossings happen, bound the overshoot, then let it shrink.

byKey.d1: You used the claim this lesson refutes. Rearranging a conditionally convergent series can change its sum.
byKey.d2: Steps can overshoot: from 1.5333 the rule jumped to 1.0333.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Divergent halves guarantee the crossings, so every term is used. The terms tending to 0 make the overshoots tend to 0. This is Riemann's rearrangement theorem for one series: any target $T$ can be reached.

screens.title: But addition commutes
screens.prose: A classmate objects: addition is commutative, so reordering cannot change a sum. The rearrangement on the first screen must still sum to $\ln 2$.
screens.question: What is wrong with the objection?

options.text: Commutativity covers finite sums. An infinite sum is a limit of partial sums, and reordering changes every partial sum.
Nothing: the dots near 1.04 are rounding error.
options.why: You blamed rounding. The gap from $\ln 2$ is about 0.35, and exact fractions give the same picture.
You doubted the rule itself. $a + b = b + a$ for all real numbers; the problem is infinitely many terms.
You thought terms were added or dropped. Every term appears exactly once.

hints.text: Commutativity is about $a + b = b + a$, two terms or any finite number.
An infinite sum is $\lim S_n$.
Reordering changes which terms are in each $S_n$, so it can change the limit.

feedback.correct: Right. Limits do not inherit commutativity for free.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what an infinite sum is defined to be.

byKey.rounding: You blamed rounding. The new sum is $\tfrac32 \ln 2 \approx 1.0397$, a full 0.35 above $\ln 2$.

explain.text: Any finite reordering keeps a finite sum. An infinite sum is the limit of partial sums, and a rearrangement has different partial sums. They may converge somewhere else, as $\tfrac32 \ln 2$ shows.

screens.title: When order cannot matter
screens.prose: **Dirichlet's theorem**: if $\sum |a_n|$ converges, every rearrangement has the same sum. The idea: choose $N$ with $\sum_{n > N} |a_n| < \varepsilon$; a late enough rearranged partial sum holds $a_1, \dots, a_N$ plus tail terms worth less than $\varepsilon$ in total. Take $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2} = \tfrac{\pi^2}{12} \approx 0.8225$.
screens.question: Why can the greedy rule not steer $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ to 1.5?

options.text: Its positive terms add to only $\tfrac{\pi^2}{8} \approx 1.2337$, so no order of the terms reaches 1.5.

options.why: You expected unlimited reach. Even every positive term together gives 1.2337, below 1.5.
You blamed the signs. $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ alternates too, and it can be steered anywhere.
You squared the signs away. The terms $\tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ keep their signs; only their sizes are squares.

hints.text: The greedy rule needs the positive half to diverge.
Here the positive half is $1 + \tfrac19 + \tfrac1{25} + \cdots$.
That sums to $\tfrac{\pi^2}{8} \approx 1.2337$, short of 1.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up all the positive terms of this series.

explain.text: Both halves converge, to $\tfrac{\pi^2}{8}$ and $-\tfrac{\pi^2}{24}$, so the greedy rule has nothing to push with. Dirichlet's theorem says more: every order gives $\tfrac{\pi^2}{12}$, because the tails are small in any order. Two positives then one negative still gives 0.822467.

screens.prose: Write `rearrange_to(target, n)`, the first $n$ terms of the greedy rearrangement of $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ aimed at `target`, as exact `Fraction`s. Compare with $\le$, exactly as the rule says.

widget.solution:
from fractions import Fraction

def rearrange_to(target, n):
    """First n terms of the greedy rearrangement of 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ...
    aimed at target, as Fractions."""
    target = Fraction(target)
    total, pos, neg, out = Fraction(0), 1, 2, []
    for _ in range(n):
        if total <= target:
            term = Fraction(1, pos)
            pos += 2
        else:
            term = Fraction(-1, neg)
            neg += 2
        total += term
        out.append(term)
    return out

tests.expect: [Fraction(1, 1), Fraction(1, 3), Fraction(1, 5), Fraction(-1, 2), Fraction(1, 7), Fraction(1, 9), Fraction(1, 11), Fraction(1, 13), Fraction(1, 15), Fraction(-1, 4), Fraction(1, 17), Fraction(1, 19)]

screens.title: Netting in what order
screens.prose: A desk nets a long list of offsetting exposures in £m: $+1, -\tfrac12, +\tfrac13, -\tfrac14, \dots$ The net in this order tends to $\ln 2 \approx$ £0.69m. The gross, $\sum |x_n|$, grows without bound. Two systems net the list in different orders and report £0.69m and £1.04m.
screens.question: Which response is right?

options.text: Insist on a finite gross before trusting any net: with infinite gross the net depends on the order of netting.

options.why: You averaged two orders. Other orders give any value at all, so the average means nothing.

options.text: Trust the system that nets in the original order.
options.why: You privileged one order. Nothing makes the listed order the true one; the gross is the problem.

options.text: The gap is floating-point error; either figure will do.
options.why: You blamed rounding. Floating-point order moves a finite total in its last digits, not by £0.35m.

hints.text: Which kind of convergence does this list have?
Conditional: the net converges, the gross $\sum \tfrac1n$ does not.
With infinite gross, Riemann's theorem says the order decides the net.

feedback.correct: Right. A net is only as trustworthy as its gross is finite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the gross is finite.

explain.text: With infinite gross the list converges only conditionally, so some order gives any net we like. With finite gross, Dirichlet's theorem makes every order agree. Even with finite totals, floating-point addition in a different order can change the last few digits.

ideas: Two positives then one negative turns $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n} = \ln 2$ into $\tfrac32 \ln 2 \approx 1.0397$: same terms, new sum.
Greedy rule: total $\le T$, take the next positive; else the next negative. Divergent halves force every crossing; shrinking terms make the overshoot vanish.
Dirichlet: if $\sum |a_n|$ converges, every order gives the same sum. Only conditional convergence can be steered.

quiz.prose: A rearrangement is to make a series sum to 10.
quiz.question: For which series is that possible?

options.why: You picked an absolutely convergent series. Dirichlet's theorem fixes its sum at $\tfrac{\pi^2}{12}$ in every order.

quiz.prose: Write $L = 1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac14 + \cdots = \ln 2$. Then $\tfrac12 L = 0 + \tfrac12 + 0 - \tfrac14 + 0 + \tfrac16 + \cdots$, with zeros spread in. Adding the two term by term gives $1 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac15 + \tfrac17 - \tfrac14 + \cdots$, the two-up-one-down order.
quiz.question: What is the sum of the two-up-one-down order?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $L$ and $\tfrac12 L$.

explain.text: Term-by-term addition of two convergent series is allowed, and the zeros change no partial-sum limits. So the new order sums to $L + \tfrac12 L = \tfrac32 \ln 2 \approx 1.039721$. That matches the dots on the first screen.
